title: They Fled Trump’s America. Now They Regret It
gist: Official data show a sharp rise in Americans moving to Europe after Trump's second-term win: US migration doubled in Q1 2025, Spain recorded a record number of US residents, Irish Foreign Births Register applications rose 63%, and UK residency applications hit their highest level since 2004. WIRED finds a growing number of these emigrants regret the move, citing lower pay, NHS costs, bureaucracy, slower work culture and Europe's own rightward drift, and some are planning to return.

themes.theme: Scale of the post-2024 US exodus

insights.claim: The number of US migrants doubled in the first quarter of 2025 compared with a year earlier, and Spain's National Statistics Institute reported a record number of American residents in 2026.
insights.speaker: Sarah Manavis
insights.so_what: Political emigration is measurable and feeds demand for relocation services, visas and rentals in Southern Europe.
insights.quote: The number of US migrants doubled in the first quarter of 2025 compared to the previous year.
insights.locator: The number of US migrants doubled

insights.claim: Citing the Financial Times, the article reports a 63% rise in American applications to Ireland's Foreign Births Register between 2024 and 2025. The UK Home office reported the most US residency applications on record (records began in 2004) for January to March 2025.
insights.speaker: Sarah Manavis
insights.so_what: Applications for ancestry-based citizenship are a leading indicator of 'exit option' hedging among wealthier Americans.
insights.locator: The Financial Times reported in April

insights.claim: In a survey of 58,000 respondents by relocation company Expats, 71% cited the US political climate as a reason for wanting to relocate.
insights.speaker: Sarah Manavis
insights.so_what: Politics, not economics, is driving this emigration wave, so it could reverse as perceptions change.

insights.claim: Digital-nomad visas introduced after the pandemic in Spain, Greece and Portugal have made it logistically easier for Americans to move.
insights.speaker: Sarah Manavis
insights.so_what: Remote-work visa regimes support demand for housing in Southern European cities, a source of local political friction.

insights.claim: American emigrants interviewed by WIRED say lower salaries leave UK residents with little disposable income. Appliances that are standard in the US, such as dishwashers and dryers, count as luxuries in the UK, and NHS care is paid for through heavy taxes plus an immigration surcharge.
insights.speaker: Sarah Manavis
insights.so_what: Gaps in income and living standards limit Europe's appeal to US talent, even when it is politically motivated.
insights.quote: I pay huge amounts of taxes and an immigration surcharge to access the NHS services—so no, the health care is not free here.

insights.claim: Returnees cite slower European work culture and bureaucracy. One says the American work style 'can get to a yes or no in less time', and another found getting work in Berlin hard because the bureaucracy had grown worse.
insights.speaker: Sarah Manavis
insights.so_what: Anecdotal support for the US advantage in labor dynamism over the EU.
insights.quote: the American work style, for better or for worse, moves much faster and can get to a yes or no in less time

insights.claim: The article attributes inflated expectations partly to social media: rosy portrayals of European life on Reddit, TikTok and Instagram set expectations that collided with reality.
insights.speaker: Sarah Manavis
insights.so_what: Narratives on social media can drive real migration decisions, and can reverse them, quickly.

insights.claim: Creators who move abroad can lose income. Leftist influencer Kate Glavan found that brands that had sponsored her lost interest once she was speaking to a British audience, and she announced a return to New York.
insights.speaker: Sarah Manavis
insights.so_what: Creator-economy income depends on the audience's geography, which limits relocation for brand-dependent creators.

themes.theme: Europe is not a political refuge

insights.claim: The article argues that Europe is not a left-wing paradise: Italy's Giorgia Meloni is a Trump ally, hard-right groups are rising in Britain, and Greece, Germany and Portugal have right-wing governments pursuing anti-immigration agendas.
insights.speaker: Sarah Manavis
insights.so_what: The rightward turn is a synchronized, transatlantic trend, which weakens the case for a political-arbitrage move.
insights.quote: The irony is that Europe is not a left-wing paradise.

insights.claim: Returnees describe online backlash on expat subreddits such as r/AmerExit and r/AmericanExpatsUK against anyone who wants to move home, and several sources stayed anonymous for fear of professional and social backlash. That suggests regret is underreported.
insights.speaker: Sarah Manavis
insights.so_what: Return migration is probably larger than public sentiment shows.
